references.text: Describes the complete ritual of the scapegoat sent to Azazel in the wilderness, where Aaron places both hands on the goat's head and confesses Israel's sins
Explains the casting of lots between the two goats—one for the Lord and one for Azazel
Mentions the man who releases the goat to Azazel and the purification rituals he must undergo afterward
Warns against offering sacrifices to goat demons (seirim), which may be connected to the concept of Azazel
The prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant who bears everyone's iniquities, parallel to the scapegoat bearing the people's sins
The suffering servant bears many sins and intercedes for transgressors, typologically fulfilled in the scapegoat ritual
Hebrews refers to the Day of Atonement and the blood brought in for unintentional sins
Christ entered the holy place once for all with his own blood and secured eternal redemption, fulfilling the rituals of the Day of Atonement
Jesus suffered outside the city gate, parallel to the scapegoat being sent outside the camp into the wilderness
John the Baptist points to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, a clear parallel to the scapegoat
Christ bore our sins in his body on the tree, fulfilling the role of the scapegoat that carried the people's sins
